title: A Modest Proposal for Preventing the Children of Poor People from Being a Burthen to Their Parents or Country, and for Making Them Beneficial to the Publick

access.edition_or_version: First published 1729; widely reprinted; public-domain text (e.g., Penguin Classics Major Works)

mechanics.premise: A fictional speaker, writing in the register of a careful political economist, proposes that the Irish poor relieve poverty by supplying their children as food to the wealthy — calculated with fiscal calm and never once flagged as horror.
mechanics.point_of_view: First-person policy persona who shares the writer's underlying concern but none of his conclusions; the mask never breaks into authorial outrage.
mechanics.style_and_devices: Deadpan bureaucratic rationality; stacked economic calculation; extension of an accepted logic to its monstrous conclusion; polite conditional phrasing held to the end.
mechanics.emotional_progression: Practical proposal -> mounting calculation -> the reader's revulsion recognized as the actual argument -> no cathartic exit, because the indictment lands on the reader's side of the table.
mechanics.conventions: Ur-text of deadpan structural satire; reference accounts note the title phrase is now conventional shorthand for that style of ironic proposal.
tone_mechanisms: deadpan mask over stated philanthropic motives
distrust converted into method (the proposal satirizes the policy logic it voices)
mechanics.critical_reception: Standard anthology piece of English prose satire; the canonical classroom example of structural irony over verbal sarcasm.
mechanics.verification_note: Existence, date (1729), authorship, fictional-narrator construction, and deadpan-satire status confirmed via Wikipedia API extract (A Modest Proposal) on 2026-09-24; voice, structure, and pacing treatment cross-checked against the repository's satirical-literature genre file, which analyzes this essay across its definition, escalation, voice, pacing, and ending sections.
